paras: The Belleview Lake revolver threat was an incident near Waterbury, Connecticut, about June 3, 1903, in which eight strike-breakers working the city's trolley lines drew revolvers on an unnamed Black man they believed had insulted them. No one was reported hurt, and the only known account came from the striking trolley men's executive committee, which used it to press the police and the company to rein in the strike-breakers.

The incident took place during a long trolley strike in Waterbury, when the strikers' executive committee issued daily statements to the press; the one reporting this episode was its 145th. The same statement mentioned strikers then on trial and the strikers' stated willingness to meet the company "halfway."

According to the committee, which said it was "reliably informed," eight strike-breakers went up to Belleview lake on the evening before the statement and saw a "colored man" scratching his head, which they took as an insult to them. The eight "pulled out revolvers and assumed attitudes of a threatening nature." The committee wrote that only the small size of the crowd at the lake kept "some hot-headed impulse" from causing bloodshed.
Afterward, the statement said, the group came down town, hired a conveyance, and drove into the outskirts firing their revolvers "in true wild west fashion."

No arrests or police action are reported in the coverage, and the man threatened is not named. The committee warned that Waterbury "will never stand for such work" and called on the police, and the employers if they could, to bring the strike-breakers in line.

The incident appeared only in the Waterbury Evening Democrat of June 4, 1903, as part of the strikers' statement printed under the headline "The Strikers' Statement" with the subhead "Tells About Some of the Skylarking of Strike Breakers." The account was framed as a complaint about "the rowdy element" among the strike-breakers rather than as an attack on a Black man, who appears only as "a colored man" and is given no name or voice. No report of the incident was found in other white papers or in the Black press.

accounts.label: Strikers' executive committee
accounts.gist: Eight strike-breakers at Belleview lake pulled revolvers on a colored man they thought had insulted them by scratching his head; only the small size of the crowd averted bloodshed, and the gang later fired revolvers 'in true wild west fashion' on the outskirts.

framing.detail: The Waterbury Evening Democrat printed the strikers' statement, which condemned the strike-breakers as 'rowdy' and urged police action; the paper's subhead called it 'Skylarking of Strike Breakers' and the incident served the strikers' case against the company's replacement workers.

record_check.dossier: A group of eight strike-breakers ('that gang'), not a crowd
Not stated in the coverage; only Waterbury and Belleview lake are named

info: The night before the 1903-06-04 statement, i.e. about 1903-06-03
Belleview lake, near Waterbury; afterward the outskirts of Waterbury
An unnamed 'colored man'; no injury reported
The strike-breakers took his scratching his head as an insult to them
Strike-breakers working on the trolley lines during the strike ('trolley chaps'), described as 'the rowdy element of that gang'

sources.note: Strikers' executive committee's 145th daily statement: eight strike-breakers drew revolvers on a colored man at Belleview lake over a supposed insult, then fired revolvers while driving through the outskirts.
quotes: got into trouble with a colored man whom they saw scratching his head and thought he did so as an insult to them
Immediately the eight trolley chaps pulled out revolvers and assumed attitudes of a threatening nature.
Luckily there was not a very big crowd around at the time or some hot-headed impulse might have been the means of causing blood-shed.
